newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tajik peace deal to be signed in Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Tajik peace deal to be signed in Moscow.

text.p: A historic peace deal between Tajikistan's government and Islamic opposition to end a civil war which has killed tens of thousands is due to be signed in the Russian capital on Friday.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin, whose health is once more the subject of speculation, and a number of foreign officals are expected to be present at the signing ceremony in the Kremlin.
For Yeltsin it will be the first public appearence since his return to Moscow on Monday after attending a summit of the Group of Seven main industrialised nations in the U.S. city of Denver.
The 66-year-old Kremlin leader, who had major heart surgery in November and pneumonia in January, spent the time since his return in a country residence working on documents, the Kremlin says.
In Denver on Saturday he missed a late-night gala concert. He resurfaced on Sunday looking well and refreshed and aides said he had just been tired after a heavy schedule of talks.
Tajik officials and observers say the planned peace accord is the first real chance of ending the war in the former Soviet republic bordering war-torn Afghanistan and China.
A ceasefire -- brokered by Iran, Russia and the United Nations -- has held for an unprecedented seven months. Earlier agreements often collapsed as soon as they were signed.
"In four years, this is the first real window onto the peace we've been waiting for," said a Tajik government official.
The planned deal was endangered by last-minute wrangling over a stalled prisoner exchange and power-sharing.

Akbar Turajonzoda, the opposition's deputy leader, was cited by the Russian news agency Interfax as saying his faction would not sign the peace agreement on Friday in Moscow unless the two issues were cleared up.
But other senior opposition officials have said this week they intend to sign the deal.
Interfax, citing Tajik government sources, said Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov might meet opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri late on Thursday to iron out the differences.
The accord envisages the creation of a 26-member National Commission for Reconciliation, to be chaired by Nuri, with places to be divided equally between each side.
Rakhmonov, who survived an assassination attempt in April, remains president but 30 percent of government posts must be given over to the opposition.
Elections for a new parliament must take place before the end of 1998. Opposition guerrillas must integrate with government forces or lay down their weapons.
But a slew of troubles cloud the guarded optimism surrounding the deal.
The inhabitants of Dushanbe are apprehensive about the return of 460 armed opposition guerrillas to the city and fear their presence could spark more fighting.

Each camp contains hardliners who have little trust for their opponents, while the power-sharing arrangement has sidelined a bewildering array of armed groups and local chieftains in the republic of 5.7 million.
With the economy in tatters, government and opposition face the immediate problem of how to deal with armed criminal bands which operate with virtual impunity throughout the republic.
